processing: Handled as raw pu-erh usually is: pan-fired, rolled, sun-dried and then pressed, with no ripening pile.
harvest_season: Spring first flush is what reaches the market under this name.
appearance_dry: Long, large leaves pressed into a cake, dark green with paler buds, as is usual for large-leaf Yiwu tea.
appearance_liquor: Golden yellow and clear, as with other young Yiwu raw teas.
appearance_wet: Large supple leaves of olive green, typical of large-leaf raw tea.
taste_profile: The seller describes a thick, sweet cup with a long buttery feel; reviewers add a lemon-zest finish and sweetness that builds over many steeps.

brewing.notes: A quick rinse, then short steeps; lengthen them gradually as the sweetness builds.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year in small spring pressings, for example a 2025 cake of 160 pieces. Few older vintages exist under this name. Availability depends on the forest rules below, so ask how the leaf was obtained.
description:
Tianmenshan, Heavenly Gate Mountain, is a forest area in the Yiwu district, not to be confused with the famous tourist mountain of the same name in Hunan. It stands apart because it lies in state forest, where picking and planting tea has come under official scrutiny.

Processing follows the usual raw pu-erh route. One small spring pressing is sold as naturally grown wild-arbor large leaf from trees of about 60 to 100 years, a seller's description rather than an independent survey.

That seller describes a thick, sweet liquor with a buttery feel, and one reviewer notes lemon zest in the finish. Beyond that, little is documented about how the tea behaves, so brew it like other young Yiwu teas: very hot water and short steeps.

Treat the name with care. Output is tiny, and authorities in Xishuangbanna have pursued illegal picking and planting in state forest. A named forest on a wrapper proves little, so favour a seller who can explain the source.
history: Little is documented about tea on Tianmenshan before recent years. A published report on Yunnan spring prices lists it among state-forest tea locations whose prices were withheld, because local agencies had begun acting against illegal picking and planting there.
